question: A student wants an RESP educational assistance payment to help cover rent and tools as well as tuition. Can the money be used for those costs, and who requests the payment?
generated_answer:
The money in an RESP can be used for various education-related expenses, including tuition, books, tools, and even living expenses while studying. To use the RESP funds for these costs, the student needs to apply for an educational assistance payment (EAP). The student is typically the one who requests the EAP from the RESP provider. The RESP provider will then review the student's enrollment in a qualifying educational program and make the payment directly to the student. 

It's important to note that there are limits to how much EAP can be taken each year, and these limits are based on the type of program and the length of study. For example, for full-time programs, the maximum EAP amount is typically 50% of the contributions made to the RESP in the first 13 weeks of the program. For part-time programs, the limit is usually 20% of contributions per 13-week period.

If you're the student and you're planning to use RESP funds for rent and tools, you should apply for an EAP as soon as you start your program. You'll need to provide proof of enrollment to the RESP provider, and they'll guide you through the process of requesting the payment. The RESP provider will then send the EAP directly to you, and you can use it to cover your eligible expenses.

In some cases, the RESP provider may have specific requirements or forms that need to be completed to request an EAP. You may also need to provide additional documentation to support your request, such as proof of residency or a detailed breakdown of your education-related expenses.

It's also worth noting that if you're planning to use RESP funds for living expenses while studying, you may need to provide additional documentation to show that these expenses are related to your education. This could include proof of residency at a student residence or a letter from your educational institution confirming that you're living off-campus for educational purposes.

Overall, as a student, you are the one who requests the EAP from the RESP provider, and you should work closely with them to ensure that you follow the correct process and meet all the necessary requirements to receive the payment. 

If you have any further questions or need more detailed guidance, I would recommend reaching out to the RESP provider directly for assistance. They will be able to provide you with specific information and support to help you make the most of your RESP funds. 

Also, remember that there are tax implications when you receive an EAP from an RESP. The amount you receive as an EAP is generally included in your income for the year and may be subject to tax. However, you may be able to claim the education tax credit on your tax return to offset some of this tax. It's a good idea to consult with a tax professional or review the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) website for more information on the tax implications of RESP EAPs. 

I hope this helps! Let me know if you have any other questions.

* [Educational assistance payments (EAPs)](https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/services/tax/individuals/topics/registered-education-savings-plans-resps/educational-assistance-payments-eaps.html)
